corrected_value.title: Improvements in problem behavior in a child with autism spectrum diagnosis through synthesized analysis and treatment: A replication in an EIBI home program.

decisions.quote:
Similar to Strand and Eldevik (2018), this study
replicated the IISCA and subsequent treatment within
an EIBI program and did not require any additional
resources or cost of the program. Differences in the
implementation of treatment included several sessions
per day (i.e., up to 28), sessions conducted as many days
of the week as possible (i.e., up to 5 days a week), and
multiple measures of social validity.
Although this study replicated the results of previous
studies (e.g., Strand and Eldevik 2018) limitations can
be noted.
decisions.location: Discussion, p. 8 (lines 1054-1064); see also Introduction, p. 2 (lines 118-129) and References, p. 10 (lines 1255-1259)
decisions.reason: Independent primary-source review confirms that Ferguson et al. (2020) empirically retests Strand and Eldevik (2018) by conducting an open-ended interview, interview-informed synthesized contingency analysis (IISCA), functional communication training, delay/denial tolerance training, compliance chaining, and parent treatment extension with an 8-year-old child with ASD in an EIBI clinic, and explicitly compares and concludes in the Discussion that it replicated Strand and Eldevik (2018)'s IISCA and treatment results within an EIBI program. The reference list (lines 1255-1259) verifies the exact citation and DOI 10.1002/bin.1505 (Behavioral Interventions, 33(1), 102-111). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 124, DOI 10.1002/jaba.106) is Hanley, Jin, Vanselow, and Hanratty (2014) in Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis (47(1), 16-36), a distinct earlier university outpatient study by a different research team; Crossref metadata and the paper's bibliography confirm that report equivalence does not apply and no duplicate target exists. Prior adjudication and Luna triage objections are resolved in favor of retaining this genuinely missing replication-original pair with outcome set to cannot_be_determined for this identity review.

decisions.reason: Independent primary-source review confirms that Hafeez and Quintana-Domeque (2018) empirically retest two specific published findings and specifications of Chakravarty (2015) using the 2006-07 Pakistan Demographic and Health Survey: (1) Chakravarty's additional sibling-sex-composition interaction hypothesis (prediction 4, Eq. 3, tested in Section V.C, Table 5 col. 5, and Section VI, Tables 11-12 col. 3, and summarized in Sections V.G and VII), confirming that girls are breastfed 0.85 months longer than boys as the elder male sibling share rises from 0 to 1, and (2) Chakravarty's quadratic birth-order interaction specification for middle-birth-order male breastfeeding advantage (Section V.F, Table 9 cols. 2-3), where replicating Chakravarty's specification in col. 2 reproduces a jointly significant interaction (p = .000) before showing in col. 3 that adding the omitted gender main effect removes the middle-birth-order peak. The reference list (p. 213) identifies Chakravarty (2015) in Journal of Applied Econometrics (30(5): 848-55) with no printed DOI. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2233, DOI 10.1093/qje/qjr029) is Jayachandran and Kuziemko (2011) on India in Quarterly Journal of Economics, a distinct earlier study by different authors; report equivalence does not apply, and sibling target 0 covers Jayachandran and Kuziemko (2011). Luna's invalid identity_quote ligature error is replaced here with a verified literal primary-source quotation, and prior scope objections are addressed.

corrected_value.title: Anxiety, depression, traumatic stress and COVID-19-related anxiety in the UK general population during the COVID-19 pandemic.

decisions.quote: Summarizing, these results are in line with those of the UK study about anxiety, depression, and traumatic stress [19]. The UK and Italian data identify factors associated with worst psychological health: being a woman, younger age, having children, preexisting health issues of self or someone close, and the moderate to high perceived risk of contracting COVID-19 within one month. Unlike Italy, in the UK lower household incomes and having (had) the COVID-19 were associated with worst psychological health outcomes.
decisions.location: Results/Discussion, Anxiety, Depression, and Traumatic Stress (lines 44-49); see also Aims (line 14), Analytic Methods Section 3.2 (line 34), and References [19] (line 288)
decisions.reason: Independent primary-source review confirms that the Italian C19PRC study explicitly retests two separate published UK C19PRC empirical papers in two distinct analytic sections: Section 3.1 (Tables 1-2) retests Shevlin et al. [20] (DOI 10.1111/bjhp.12430) on COVID-19 anxiety quintiles predicting PHQ-15 somatic symptoms, whereas Section 3.2 (Tables 3-5, lines 34, 41-49) explicitly replicates the three binary logistic regression models of Shevlin et al. [19] (DOI 10.1192/bjo.2020.109) predicting moderate anxiety/depression (GAD-7/PHQ-9), traumatic stress (ITQ), and high COVID-19-related anxiety from sociodemographic and health risk factors, and directly compares which risk factors matched or differed between the UK and Italian samples. Reference [19] (line 288) and Crossref metadata verify Shevlin et al. (2020) in BJPsych Open (6, DOI 10.1192/bjo.2020.109). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 259, DOI 10.1111/bjhp.12430, corresponding to sibling target_index 1) is the British Journal of Health Psychology somatic-symptoms article [20]; although both UK papers analyze wave 1 of the UK C19PRC survey, they test distinct dependent variables, statistical models, and substantive claims and are not preliminary/full reports of the same original finding.

decisions.quote:
Our results replicate both the original Coleman Report
ICCs, as well as those from Bryk and Raudenbush’s study. In the left column of Table 1 (variation in
achievement levels), our results are largely consistent with the Coleman Report: Only 23.7% of the
variance in math achievement levels lies between schools (21.4% in ELA). When it comes to linear
growth rates (middle panel of Table 1), our results are quite similar to the surprising findings from
Bryk and Raudenbush: The majority—73.5%—of the variance in math learning rates lies between
schools (80.7% in ELA).
decisions.location: Results, p. 5 (lines 147-154); see also Current Analysis, p. 4 (lines 134-137), Table 1, p. 10 (lines 263-277), and References, p. 13 (lines 329-331)
decisions.reason: Independent primary-source review confirms that Atteberry and McEachin (2020) do not merely cite Coleman et al. (1966) as historical background: in Current Analysis (p. 4), Results (p. 5), and Table 1 (p. 10), they estimate between-school intraclass correlations (ICCs) for student achievement levels using NWEA MAP data across grades 1-8 and explicitly compare and replicate the Coleman Report's achievement-level ICCs from Table 3.21.5 (reporting 23.7% math and 21.4% ELA between-school achievement-level variance alongside Coleman's 9.0%-20.9% across grades 3, 6, and 9). Addressing the prior pilot objection directly, explicit empirical retesting and side-by-side tabular comparison in Results establish Coleman et al. (1966) as a replicated target despite Introduction discussion. The reference list (p. 13) verifies Coleman, J. S., Campbell, E., Hobson, C., McPartland, F., Mood, A., & Weinfeld, F. (1966), Equality of educational opportunity study, with no printed DOI. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 16, DOI 10.1016/b978-0-12-108840-8.50014-7, corresponding to sibling target_index 1 for Bryk & Raudenbush 1988/1989) is a distinct later multilevel growth-rate study by different authors; report equivalence does not apply.
